title: Overview and justification
body:
This short course is about academic integrity: what it really is, why referencing matters so much to it, and how to use sources with the judgement that integrity asks for. It assumes you can already reference accurately, and steps back to the principles that referencing serves. By the end you will be able to articulate what academic integrity means, justify why referencing matters beyond avoiding plagiarism, and judge how to quote and paraphrase sources with integrity.

These are not box-ticking concerns. Integrity is what makes academic work trustworthy, and the ability to use sources with judgement is what separates confident scholarly writing from anxious rule-following. Owning it now carries into your dissertation, and into any professional work where your word has to be relied on.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this course, you will be able to:

_items.text: articulate what academic integrity means and the values that underpin it
justify why referencing matters as scholarly practice, beyond avoiding plagiarism
judge when to quote and when to paraphrase, and use sources with integrity.

title: In real academic practice
body: Academic integrity is the ground every piece of academic work stands on. Each essay you reference with purpose, each source you weigh rather than stack, each judgement about quoting or paraphrasing, is integrity in practice. Build the habit of owning it now and it carries through your degree and into professional work, where being trusted with the truth is the whole point.

title: Signpost
body: The course has three short lessons. First, academic integrity and its values: what you are really being asked to hold. Second, why referencing matters: the scholarly work a reference does, beyond keeping you out of trouble. Third, using sources with integrity: the judgement involved in quoting and paraphrasing well. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.

title: Course instructions
body:
Start and finish with a confidence check. Before the lessons, you'll rate how confident you feel about each part of this topic. You'll rate the same statements again at the end, so you can see what has changed. Your ratings are yours: they aren't marked and no one else sees them.

The activities in the lessons are for practice. Questions, examples and reflective prompts are there to help you think, and they don't count towards passing. Reflective prompts are private and optional.

The test at the end is the one that counts. To complete the course you need to take the final test and score at least 70%. You can retake it.

title: How this course works
body:
The examples and activities in this course use invented people, authors and sources to show how things work. Unless we say otherwise, any name, citation or reference you meet in an example is fictional.

Where a lesson draws on real work, you'll find it listed under Lesson Sources at the bottom of that page. Every real source used in the course is gathered under Course Sources at the end.

title: Orientation
body: You already know how to reference: what a reference is made of, which style your subject uses, how to cite a source when you quote or paraphrase it. This course steps back from the mechanics to the thing they serve. Referencing is the most visible part of academic integrity, and academic integrity is best understood not as a set of rules but as a set of values that scholarly work holds in common.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this level the aim is not to be told the rules again, but to articulate the principles for yourself. A student who can say why integrity matters, and judge a difficult case against its values, is better placed than one who has only memorised what is and is not allowed. That is the move this lesson asks of you.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: articulate what academic integrity means as a set of shared scholarly values rather than a list of rules
explain how a value such as honesty, trust or responsibility shows up in everyday academic work
appraise a situation in {{context}} against the values of academic integrity.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Academic integrity is often introduced through its breaches: do not plagiarise, do not fabricate, do not cheat. Defined that way it looks like a rulebook. It is better understood as a set of values that scholarly communities hold in common. A widely recognised framework names six shared values: honesty, trust, fairness, respect, responsibility, and the courage to act on the others when it is difficult.

Seen this way, referencing is not a hoop to jump through but one expression of those values. When you reference a source you are being honest about whose ideas you are using, showing respect for the work of others, and taking responsibility for the claims you make. The rules follow from the values; the values are what you are really being asked to hold.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of a time when acting with integrity in your work was not the easiest option. What value was at stake, and what did you do?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
body: Academic integrity is best understood not as a rulebook but as a set of shared scholarly values: honesty, trust, fairness, respect, responsibility and courage. Referencing is one visible expression of those values rather than a hoop to clear. You can now articulate what integrity means, explain how a value shows up in real academic work, and appraise a difficult situation against the values. The next lesson turns to why referencing in particular matters so much.

title: Orientation
body: If referencing were only about avoiding plagiarism, you could satisfy it mechanically and think no more about it. In fact a reference does a great deal of positive work in a piece of academic writing. This lesson is about that work: what a reader actually learns from your references, and why experienced scholars treat them as part of the argument rather than an afterthought.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You can already reference accurately. The step at this level is to be able to defend your referencing: to say what each citation is doing for the reader and the argument, so that you cite with purpose rather than from habit or from fear of a penalty.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: justify referencing as the way you join, credit and are credited within a scholarly conversation
explain how references signal the scope and the critical edge of your research to a reader
defend the value of referencing a source in {{context}} beyond avoiding plagiarism.

title: Concept: definition
body:
A piece of academic writing is a contribution to an ongoing conversation among scholars, and references are how you take part in it. They credit the people whose work you build on, and in turn they let others credit you when they build on yours. Without them the conversation could not accumulate.

References also tell the reader a great deal at a glance. The range of sources shows the scope of your research: how widely and how deeply you have read. The way you use them shows your critical edge: whether you merely cite authorities or weigh them against one another. A tutor reading your citations is reading evidence of how you think, not only checking that you have not copied.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Look back at a recent reference list of your own. What does it tell a reader about the scope and the critical edge of your reading?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
body: Referencing does far more than keep you clear of plagiarism. It credits the scholars you build on and lets others credit you, so that the scholarly conversation can accumulate. It also signals, at a glance, the scope of your reading and the critical edge of your thinking. You can now justify referencing as joining a conversation, explain what references tell a reader, and defend referencing on grounds stronger than fear of a penalty. The last lesson turns to the judgement involved in using sources well.

title: Orientation
body: Quoting and paraphrasing are the two ways you bring a source's words into your own writing, and choosing between them is a matter of judgement, not a rule. Paraphrase carelessly and you can drift into the source's own words without meaning to, which is where honest intentions still produce a breach. This lesson is about using sources so that the integrity holds.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You already know how to cite a quotation and a paraphrase. The step here is judgement: deciding which to use and when, and recognising the point at which a paraphrase stays so close to the original that it is no longer your own expression, however carefully it is cited.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: judge when to quote a source directly and when to paraphrase it
distinguish a sound paraphrase from one that stays too close to the source's words
decide how to handle a source in {{context}} so that its use keeps academic integrity.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Quoting reproduces a source's exact words in quotation marks; paraphrasing restates its meaning in your own. Each has its place. You quote when the precise wording matters: a definition, a memorable phrase, or a claim you intend to examine closely. You paraphrase, which is the more common move, when you want the idea in the flow of your own argument and in your own voice.

Paraphrase is also the harder move to do with integrity. A sound paraphrase rebuilds the idea in genuinely different words and structure, and still cites the source. A weak one swaps a few words while keeping the original's shape and phrasing. The second is sometimes called patchwriting, and even with a citation attached it fails, because the expression is not your own. Doing paraphrase well is how you show that you have understood, not merely relocated, what you read.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think about how you usually decide between quoting and paraphrasing. Is it a judgement about the source, or a habit? What might you change?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
body: Using a source well is a matter of judgement. You quote when the exact wording matters and paraphrase, the more common move, when you want the idea in your own voice. A sound paraphrase rebuilds the idea in genuinely new words and structure and cites the source; a paraphrase that only swaps a few words stays the source's expression and fails even when cited. You can now judge between quoting and paraphrasing, tell a sound paraphrase from one too close to the source, and decide how to handle a source so that its integrity holds. With the values, the reasons and the judgement in place, referencing is something you can own and defend.

title: Course summary
body: You have reached the end of the course. Academic integrity is no longer a rulebook but a set of values you can name and defend: honesty, trust, fairness, respect, responsibility and courage. You can articulate what integrity means and how it shows up in practice. You can justify why referencing matters as scholarly work, crediting a conversation and signalling the scope and critical edge of your reading, not merely avoiding plagiarism. And you can judge when to quote and when to paraphrase, and tell sound source use from a breach. Look back at the confidence check: comparing where you started with where you are now shows how far this has moved.

title: In real academic practice
body: From here, integrity is something you practise in every piece of work. Each source you reference with purpose, each judgement about quoting or paraphrasing, each difficult case you handle by the values, is integrity owned rather than obeyed. It is also what professional life depends on: being someone whose account of where knowledge came from can be trusted.

title: Course Sources
instruction: This course draws on the following source.

_items.title: See pages 184 to 199 of Chapter 10, 'Academic Integrity and Referencing', of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

title: Explore the concept
body: Academic integrity is usually taught as a list of don'ts. Underneath sit six values that scholarly communities share. Read each card to see the value the rules are really protecting.
instruction: Read through the cards below.
ariaRegion: Information cards on the values of academic integrity.

_items.title: Honesty
_items.subtitle: What is mine, what is others'
_items.text: Being truthful about which ideas are your own and which you have drawn from others. Referencing is honesty made visible: it shows exactly whose thinking sits behind your argument.

_items.title: Trust
_items.subtitle: The ground scholarship stands on
_items.text: Readers trust that your sources are real, your data genuine, and your words your own unless marked otherwise. Every accurate reference keeps that trust intact.

_items.title: Fairness
_items.subtitle: To scholars and to peers
_items.text: Crediting other scholars fairly, and being assessed on comparable terms with other students. Integrity protects both kinds of fairness at once.

_items.title: Respect
_items.subtitle: For work and for readers
_items.text: Respect for the people whose work you build on, and for the readers who rely on your account. Citing a source respects the labour and thought it represents.

_items.title: Responsibility
_items.subtitle: Owning your claims
_items.text: Taking responsibility for the claims you make and the sources you stand on. You own your argument, including the places where it leans on someone else's.

_items.title: Courage
_items.subtitle: When it would be easier not to
_items.text: The courage to uphold the other values when it is hard: to attribute an idea you wish were your own, or to raise a concern about a breach you have seen.

title: Worked example
body:
Consider two students writing up an idea they first met in a seminar reading.

{{learner-a}} likes the idea, rephrases it, and builds a paragraph around it without naming where it came from. Nothing is copied word for word, so it feels safe. But the reader is left to assume the thinking is {{learner-a}}'s own. The omission is not a formatting slip; it quietly breaks the honesty and trust the work depends on.

{{learner-b}} uses the same idea but attributes it to its author, then adds a line of their own about what it does and does not establish. The reference is not defensive cover; it is {{learner-b}} being honest about the debt, respectful of the author, and responsible for the further claim. The paragraph is stronger for it, because the reader can see exactly where {{learner-b}}'s own contribution begins.

Both students used the idea well. Only {{learner-b}} treated referencing as an expression of the values, rather than a rule to be managed.

title: Holding the values
body: These questions turn the values from words into something you can check your own practice against.
instruction: Tick each item once you have considered it.

_items.text: Have I been honest about which ideas are mine and which I have drawn from others?
Would a reader trust that every source I name is real and used fairly?
Have I credited the scholars whose work my argument stands on?
Have I taken responsibility for the claims I make, including the borrowed ones?
Where a case was difficult, did I act on the values rather than take the easy route?
Could I explain, in terms of the values, why I referenced the way I did?

title: Formative check: what integrity is
displayTitle: Which statement best captures what academic integrity is?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which statement best captures what academic integrity is?

_items.text: A set of shared scholarly values, such as honesty and trust, that the rules and referencing express.
_items.feedback: Yes. The values come first; the rules follow from them.

_items.text: A list of prohibited actions that students must memorise to avoid penalties.
_items.feedback: That is how breaches are policed, but it mistakes the rules for the thing itself.

_items.text: A formatting standard that makes references consistent across a piece of work.
_items.feedback: Formatting is a mechanic of referencing, not what integrity is.

_items.text: A disciplinary process for dealing with plagiarism after it has happened.
_items.feedback: That is the response to a breach, not the value being protected.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Academic integrity is the values that scholarship shares; the rules and referencing are how those values are expressed.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look past the rules and penalties to what they are there to protect.
_incorrect.final: Academic integrity is a set of shared scholarly values, such as honesty and trust. The rules, the formatting and the disciplinary process all follow from those values rather than being integrity itself.

title: Formative check: a value in practice
displayTitle: In the worked example, what was the real problem with the first student's paragraph?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What was the real problem with the first student's paragraph?

_items.text: By not attributing the idea, they let the reader assume borrowed thinking was their own, breaking honesty and trust.
_items.feedback: Yes. The missing attribution is a breach of the values, not a formatting slip.

_items.text: They rephrased the idea instead of quoting it directly.
_items.feedback: Rephrasing is fine; the problem was the missing attribution.

_items.text: They used an idea from a seminar reading rather than from a journal.
_items.feedback: Where the idea came from is not the issue; failing to credit it is.

_items.text: They added a line of their own about what the idea established.
_items.feedback: That is what the second student did well, not the first student's problem.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The breach was in letting borrowed thinking pass as their own, which is where honesty and trust give way.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what the reader was left to assume, and which values that affects.
_incorrect.final: The problem was that the idea went unattributed, so the reader assumed the thinking was the student's own. That breaks honesty and trust, whatever the formatting looks like.

title: Formative check: appraising a situation
displayTitle: You are working in {{context}} and find a claim in your draft that came from a source you can no longer locate. Which response best fits the values of academic integrity?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which response best fits the values when you cannot locate a source?

_items.text: Treat the claim as a debt you cannot yet honour: track the source down, or set the claim aside until you can attribute it.
_items.feedback: Yes. That keeps faith with honesty and responsibility in {{context}}.

_items.text: Leave the claim unreferenced, since you cannot prove where it came from anyway.
_items.feedback: Leaving borrowed thinking unattributed is the breach the values warn against.

_items.text: Attribute it to a different source on the same topic so that a reference is present.
_items.feedback: A false attribution breaks honesty more seriously than a missing one.

_items.text: Keep it but reword it heavily so that no reference seems necessary.
_items.feedback: Rewording to hide a debt is exactly what integrity asks you not to do.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, honesty and responsibility mean honouring the debt or holding the claim back until you can.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which option keeps faith with honesty and responsibility, rather than hiding or faking the debt?
_incorrect.final: The values point to tracking the source down or setting the claim aside. Leaving it unattributed, faking an attribution, or rewording to hide the debt all breach honesty in {{context}}.

title: Explore the concept
body: Ask what a single reference achieves and the answers run deeper the longer you look. Reveal each stage to move from the reason students meet first to the reason scholars care about most.
instruction: Select each stage to reveal what a reference is doing at that depth.

_items.title: Avoiding plagiarism
_items.body: The reason most students meet first: a reference shows an idea is not being passed off as your own. True, but it is the floor, not the point.

_items.title: Giving credit
_items.body: A reference credits the scholar whose work you used. Scholarship is cumulative, and crediting others is how the whole enterprise keeps faith with itself.

_items.title: Showing your scope
_items.body: Your sources, taken together, show how widely and how well you have read. The reference list is quiet evidence of the research behind the argument.

_items.title: Showing your critical edge
_items.body: How you use sources, setting them against one another rather than stacking them up, shows the reader you are weighing the field, not just gathering it.

_items.title: Joining the conversation
_items.body: At its fullest, referencing is how you enter a scholarly conversation: crediting those before you, and leaving a trail others can follow and credit in turn.

title: Worked example
body:
Two students submit essays that both avoid plagiarism and both reference correctly.

{{learner-a}} cites a source after almost every sentence, each one a well-known authority, each dropped in to back a point already made. The citations are accurate and the list is long. But they all pull the same way: nothing is set against anything else, so the reader sees reading, not thinking. The references prove {{learner-a}} did the reading, and little more.

{{learner-b}} cites fewer sources but uses them against one another: one author is introduced, then qualified by a second who disagrees, and the paragraph reaches a position of its own. The same conventions now carry a visibly critical argument. The reader can see {{learner-b}} weighing the field, not just reporting it.

Both reference correctly. Only {{learner-b}} made the references work as evidence of thinking, which is what they are for.

title: Making references work
body: Use these questions to check that your references are doing scholarly work, not just satisfying a rule.
instruction: Tick each item once you have considered it.

_items.text: Can I say what each citation is doing for the argument, not just that it is accurate?
Do my sources, taken together, show the scope of my reading?
Have I set sources against one another anywhere, rather than only stacking agreement?
Would my reference list give a reader a fair picture of the conversation I am joining?
Have I credited the thinking I built on, not only the words I quoted?
Am I citing with purpose, rather than from habit or fear of a penalty?

title: Formative check: why referencing matters
displayTitle: Beyond avoiding plagiarism, what is the fullest justification for referencing in the view this lesson takes?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What is the fullest justification for referencing beyond avoiding plagiarism?

_items.text: It lets you join a scholarly conversation: crediting those you build on, and letting others credit you in turn.
_items.feedback: Yes. That is referencing at its fullest.

_items.text: It makes an essay look longer and more authoritative to the marker.
_items.feedback: Appearance is not the point; the scholarly work a reference does is.

_items.text: It guarantees a higher mark by increasing the number of sources cited.
_items.feedback: More citations do not earn marks by themselves; how you use sources does.

_items.text: It transfers responsibility for any weak claims onto the authors you cite.
_items.feedback: Referencing does not shift responsibility; you still own your argument.

_feedback.correct: That's right. At its fullest, referencing is how you take part in an accumulating scholarly conversation.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the reason that goes beyond appearance, marks or shifting blame.
_incorrect.final: The fullest justification is that referencing lets you join a scholarly conversation, crediting others and being credited in turn. Length, mark-chasing and shifting blame are not what references are for.

title: Formative check: critical edge
displayTitle: In the worked example, why did the second student's references show a stronger critical edge than the first's?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why did the second student's references show a stronger critical edge?

_items.text: They set sources against one another to reach a position, rather than citing authorities that all agreed.
_items.feedback: Yes. Weighing sources against each other is what the critical edge looks like.

_items.text: They cited far more sources than the first student did.
_items.feedback: The second student cited fewer, not more; it was the use that differed.

_items.text: They placed a citation after almost every sentence.
_items.feedback: That describes the first student's stacking, which showed reading not thinking.

_items.text: They chose more famous authorities than the first student.
_items.feedback: Fame of the sources is not the point; how they were weighed is.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Setting sources against one another, rather than stacking agreement, is the critical edge a reader can see.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what the second student did with the sources, not how many there were.
_incorrect.final: The critical edge came from setting sources against one another to reach a position. Citing more, citing after every sentence, or citing famous names does not show thinking by itself.

title: Formative check: defending referencing
displayTitle: A peer studying {{context}} says they reference only to stay out of trouble. Which reply best defends referencing on stronger grounds?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which reply best defends referencing on stronger grounds than staying out of trouble?

_items.text: Your references also show the scope and critical edge of your reading, and credit the scholars whose conversation you are joining.
_items.feedback: Yes. That is the fuller case for referencing in {{context}}.

_items.text: Staying out of trouble is genuinely the only reason to reference, and no deeper case exists.
_items.feedback: That is the floor this lesson argues past.

_items.text: You should reference less, then, so that markers do not scrutinise your sources.
_items.feedback: Referencing less hides the scholarly work references do.

_items.text: Referencing only matters in subjects that use a named citation style.
_items.feedback: The scholarly reasons hold across subjects, whatever the style.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, references show scope and critical edge and credit a conversation, which is the stronger case.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the reply that gives referencing positive scholarly work to do.
_incorrect.final: The stronger defence is that references signal the scope and critical edge of your reading and credit the conversation you join. Those reasons hold in {{context}} whatever the citation style.

title: Explore the concept
body: A student has paraphrased a source and cited it. One part is genuinely in their own words; one stays too close to the original's phrasing; one is the citation. Judge which is which.
instruction: Choose a tool, then select the matching part of the passage. Mark all three, then Submit.
ariaRegion: Annotate. Choose a tool, then select parts of the passage to mark their role.
passage: The review found that remote teams [[coordinate differently when they cannot meet face to face]], a [[fundamental reconfiguration of collaborative work]], according to [[(Hughes, 2020)]].

_feedback.correct: Exactly. You have told the genuinely reworded part from the phrase lifted too close to the source, and found the citation.
_feedback._incorrect: Not quite. The plain, everyday wording is the student's own; the polished academic phrase reads as lifted from the source; the bracketed name is the citation.

title: Worked example
body:
Two students want to use the same sentence from a source in their essays.

{{learner-a}} decides to paraphrase, but stays close to the original: a few words are swapped for synonyms while the sentence keeps its shape and its distinctive phrasing. A citation is added, so it feels above board. Yet the expression is still the source's, not {{learner-a}}'s. Cited or not, this patchwriting shows the words were moved, not the idea understood.

{{learner-b}} judges that the source's exact wording is not what matters here, only the idea, so paraphrase is the right move. They set the source aside, write the point from memory in their own words, then check back to confirm the meaning holds and the wording is genuinely their own. The source is cited. The paraphrase shows understanding, because it is rebuilt rather than relabelled.

Both cited the source. Only {{learner-b}} made a judgement about how to use it that kept the integrity intact.

title: Using a source well
body: Run a source you are about to use past these questions before you commit to quoting or paraphrasing it.
instruction: Tick each item once you have considered it.

_items.text: Have I decided between quoting and paraphrasing for a reason, not by default?
If I quoted, is it because the exact wording matters?
If I paraphrased, did I rebuild the idea in my own words and structure, not just swap a few words?
Did I set the source aside and write from understanding, then check back?
Is the expression genuinely mine, even though the idea is cited?
Would this paraphrase still stand if the citation were removed and it were judged as my own writing?

title: Formative check: quote or paraphrase
displayTitle: When is quoting a source directly the better judgement, rather than paraphrasing?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: When is quoting directly the better judgement than paraphrasing?

_items.text: When the exact wording matters, such as a precise definition or a phrase you intend to examine closely.
_items.feedback: Yes. Quote when the wording itself is doing the work.

_items.text: Whenever you are short of time to put the idea into your own words.
_items.feedback: Saving time is not a sound reason to quote.

_items.text: Whenever the source is written more clearly than you could manage.
_items.feedback: That is a reason to work on your paraphrase, not to quote.

_items.text: Whenever you want to raise the number of citations in your essay.
_items.feedback: Citation count is not a reason to quote rather than paraphrase.

_feedback.correct: That's right. You quote when the exact wording matters; otherwise paraphrase is usually the better move.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about when the words themselves, not just the idea, need to be on the page.
_incorrect.final: Quoting is the better judgement when the exact wording matters, such as a definition or a phrase you will examine. Time, the source's clarity and citation count are not sound reasons to quote.

title: Formative check: sound or too close
displayTitle: In the worked example, why did the first student's paraphrase fail even though it was cited?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why did the first student's paraphrase fail even though it was cited?

_items.text: It kept the source's shape and phrasing with only a few words swapped, so the expression was still the source's, not their own.
_items.feedback: Yes. A citation does not rescue expression that is still the source's.

_items.text: It paraphrased an idea that should have been quoted directly instead.
_items.feedback: The choice to paraphrase was fine; the execution was the problem.

_items.text: It cited the wrong source for the sentence being used.
_items.feedback: The citation was not the issue; the closeness of the wording was.

_items.text: It was shorter than the original sentence from the source.
_items.feedback: Length is not what made it fail.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Patchwriting keeps the source's expression, and a citation does not make it the student's own work.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about whose words the paragraph really contained, citation aside.
_incorrect.final: The paraphrase failed because it kept the source's shape and phrasing with only words swapped, so the expression was still the source's. A citation cannot make lifted expression your own work.

title: Formative check: handling a source
displayTitle: You are using a key source in {{context}} whose precise wording does not matter to your point, only its idea. Which handling keeps academic integrity?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which handling of the source keeps academic integrity?

_items.text: Paraphrase it: rebuild the idea in your own words and structure from your understanding, and cite the source.
_items.feedback: Yes. That is the sound judgement in {{context}} when only the idea matters.

_items.text: Quote it in full, since quoting is always the safest way to avoid a breach.
_items.feedback: Quoting when only the idea matters clutters your argument and is not safer.

_items.text: Reword a few of its terms while keeping its sentence, and add a citation.
_items.feedback: That is patchwriting; the citation does not rescue it.

_items.text: Use the idea without a citation, because you have put it into your own words.
_items.feedback: Own words still need a citation when the idea is someone else's.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, rebuild the idea in your own words and structure and cite it.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which option both makes the expression genuinely yours and still credits the source?
_incorrect.final: When only the idea matters, paraphrase properly and cite the source. Quoting in full, swapping a few words, or dropping the citation all fail the judgement in {{context}}.

body: Which statement best describes academic integrity?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which statement best describes academic integrity?

_items.text: A set of shared scholarly values, such as honesty, trust and responsibility, that the rules and referencing express.
_items.feedback: Yes. The values are what integrity is.

_items.text: A list of prohibited actions students memorise to avoid penalties.
_items.feedback: That mistakes the rules for the values they protect.

_items.text: A formatting standard that keeps references consistent.
_items.feedback: That is a mechanic of referencing, not integrity.

_items.text: A disciplinary process that deals with plagiarism.
_items.feedback: That responds to a breach; it is not what integrity is.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Academic integrity is a set of shared scholarly values.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look past the rules to the values they protect.

body: Why is it fair to call referencing an expression of academic integrity, rather than a separate rule?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is referencing an expression of integrity rather than a separate rule?

_items.text: Because referencing enacts the values: being honest about your sources, crediting others, and owning your claims.
_items.feedback: Yes. Referencing is the values in action.

_items.text: Because referencing is harder to do than the other rules.
_items.feedback: Difficulty is not why it expresses the values.

_items.text: Because referencing is the only rule that carries a penalty.
_items.feedback: It is not the only rule, and penalties are not the point.

_items.text: Because referencing applies only to direct quotations.
_items.feedback: Referencing applies well beyond direct quotation.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Referencing enacts honesty, credit and responsibility.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about which values a reference actually puts into practice.

body: Beyond avoiding plagiarism, what does a reference list tell a reader about your work?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does a reference list tell a reader beyond avoiding plagiarism?

_items.text: The scope of your reading and, in how the sources are used, the critical edge of your thinking.
_items.feedback: Yes. A reference list is evidence of scope and critical edge.

_items.text: Only that you have not copied anyone else's words.
_items.feedback: That is the floor; references do far more.

_items.text: The exact mark your essay deserves.
_items.feedback: A reference list does not set a mark.

_items.text: That you prefer well-known authorities to recent work.
_items.feedback: That is not what a reference list is there to show.

_feedback.correct: That's right. References signal the scope and critical edge of your reading.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what a reader learns from the range and use of your sources.

body: What is the fullest reason this course gives for referencing?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What is the fullest reason for referencing?

_items.text: It is how you join a scholarly conversation, crediting those you build on and letting others credit you.
_items.feedback: Yes. That is referencing at its fullest.

_items.text: It makes an essay look more authoritative.
_items.feedback: Appearance is not the fullest reason.

_items.text: It raises your mark by adding more sources.
_items.feedback: More sources do not raise marks by themselves.

_items.text: It shifts responsibility for weak claims onto your sources.
_items.feedback: Referencing does not transfer responsibility.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Referencing is how you join and sustain a scholarly conversation.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the reason about the scholarly conversation.

body: When is paraphrasing the better choice than quoting?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: When is paraphrasing the better choice than quoting?

_items.text: When the idea matters more than the exact wording and you want it in your own voice.
_items.feedback: Yes. Paraphrase when the idea, not the wording, is what you need.

_items.text: When you are short of time to think about the wording.
_items.feedback: Time pressure is not a sound basis for the choice.

_items.text: When you want to increase the number of quotations.
_items.feedback: Paraphrasing does not increase quotations.

_items.text: When the source is too clearly written to quote.
_items.feedback: Clarity of the source is not the deciding factor.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Paraphrase when the idea matters more than the exact wording.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about whether the wording itself needs to be on the page.

body: A paraphrase swaps a few words but keeps the source's sentence shape and phrasing, with a citation attached. How should this be judged?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: How should a lightly reworded, cited paraphrase be judged?

_items.text: As a breach: the expression is still the source's, so a citation does not make it the student's own work.
_items.feedback: Yes. Patchwriting fails even when cited.

_items.text: As sound, because a citation is present.
_items.feedback: A citation does not rescue lifted expression.

_items.text: As sound, because some words were changed.
_items.feedback: Swapping a few words leaves the expression the source's.

_items.text: As sound, because the idea came from a real source.
_items.feedback: Using a real source is not the issue; the expression is.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Patchwriting is a breach even with a citation, because the expression is not the student's own.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about whose expression the sentence still carries.

title: Orientation
body: You have now looked at three things: what academic integrity is, why referencing matters as scholarly work, and the judgement in using sources well. On their own they are three separate ideas. This lesson brings them together into one practice you can keep using.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this stage the aim is not to run through the three ideas again. It is to see them as one practice rather than three separate ideas, so that it carries on past this course and into the rest of your studies.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: bring together the values of academic integrity, the reasons referencing matters, and the judgement in using sources into one practice
recognise academic integrity at work as one practice in how a student handles a source
plan how you will use sources with integrity in your {{context}} work beyond this course

title: Concept: definition
body: Academic integrity in practice is the three strands working as one. Each time you use a source, you hold the shared values, you reference with purpose, and you judge how to quote or paraphrase. The values guide the judgement, the judgement puts the values into action, and the reference is where both become visible to a reader.

title: Concept: in practice
body: In practice, this is something you do with every source, in any subject. For each source you make a short, deliberate pass: which values are at stake, why you are citing it, and how best to use it. Over an assignment, those small judgements add up to work a reader can trust.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of a piece of work coming up in your studies. Which part of this practice do you most want to carry forward: holding the values, referencing with purpose, or judging how to use a source? Name one, and say how you will do it.
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and the questions have no right answers.

title: Summary
body: Using sources with integrity is most useful when it becomes one continuing practice. With each source you hold the values, reference with purpose, and judge how to quote or paraphrase, again and again. It is the habit, carried across your work, that makes your scholarship trustworthy.

title: Lesson Sources
instruction: This lesson draws on the following sources.

_items.title: See pages 42 to 43 of Chapter 3 of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).
See pages 73 to 74 of Chapter 5 of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).
See pages 93 to 94 of Chapter 6 of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

title: The practice as one cycle
body: Academic integrity in practice is one continuing cycle, run each time you use a source. Select each part to see what it involves.
instruction: Select each part of the cycle.

_items.title: Recognise
_items.body: Recognise which values are at stake in how you use this source.

_items.title: Decide
_items.body: Decide why the source belongs in your argument and what its reference will do.

_items.title: Judge
_items.body: Judge whether to quote or paraphrase it, and put it in your own voice.

_items.title: Reference and carry
_items.body: Reference it accurately, then carry the same practice to your next source. The cycle keeps turning.

_diagram.title: Academic integrity as a continuing practice

title: Worked example
body: Two students use the same source in an essay. One drops in a citation at the end, correct but unconsidered, and moves on. The other pauses to weigh which values are at stake, decides a paraphrase serves the argument better than a quote, and references it to credit the author. Over the essay, the second student's sources read as thinking, not just proof that the reading was done.

title: Working with the cycle
displayTitle: How to use every source with integrity
body: Use these questions to keep integrity turning as one practice, rather than treating each source as a fresh start.
instruction: Tick each item when you have done it.

_items.text: Have I recognised which values are at stake in how I use this source?
Can I say what this reference does for my argument, beyond avoiding plagiarism?
Have I judged whether to quote or paraphrase, rather than defaulting to habit?
If I paraphrased, is the wording genuinely my own and not the source's shape reworded?
Would my finished reference let a reader see the values and the judgement behind it?

displayTitle: Why is it better to treat academic integrity as one scholarly practice rather than three separate ideas?
body: Why is it better to treat academic integrity as one scholarly practice rather than three separate ideas?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is it better to treat academic integrity as one scholarly practice rather than three separate ideas?

_items.text: Because the three work together on every source: the values guide the judgement, the judgement puts the values into action, and the reference makes both visible.
_items.feedback: Yes. The values, the reasons and the judgement are one practice, not three separate tasks.

_items.text: Because learning three separate ideas is harder than learning one.
_items.feedback: The point is not that one idea is easier. It is that the three act together on every source.

_items.text: Because the values matter and the reasons and the judgement do not.
_items.feedback: All three matter. The practice is holding them together, not choosing between them.

_items.text: Because treating it as one practice means you can skip referencing accurately.
_items.feedback: Accurate referencing is where the practice becomes visible; it is never skipped.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The values, the reasons referencing matters, and the judgement in using sources are one practice that runs on every source.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the reason the three ideas belong together on every source you use.

displayTitle: A student weighs whether to quote or paraphrase a source. They rework it in their own words, because the idea matters more than the wording, and reference it to credit the author and show their reading. What does this show?
body: A student weighs whether to quote or paraphrase a source. They rework it in their own words, because the idea matters more than the wording, and reference it to credit the author and show their reading. What does this show?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A student weighs whether to quote or paraphrase a source. They rework it in their own words, because the idea matters more than the wording, and reference it to credit the author and show their reading. What does this show?

_items.text: Integrity working as one practice: the values, the reasons for referencing, and the judgement about using the source are all in play at once.
_items.feedback: Yes. The student held the values, referenced with purpose, and judged how to use the source, together.

_items.text: That the student quoted the source directly to keep its exact wording.
_items.feedback: They paraphrased, judging that the idea mattered more than the wording.

_items.text: That referencing is only about avoiding plagiarism.
_items.feedback: The reference here also credits the author and shows the student's reading.

_items.text: That the values and the judgement are separate from the reference.
_items.feedback: The reference is where the values and the judgement become visible; they are not separate.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Holding the values, referencing with purpose, and judging how to use the source are one practice, seen here on a single source.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Notice how the student used the values, the purpose and the judgement on the same source at once.

displayTitle: You want to use what you have learned to handle sources with integrity in your {{context}} work this term. Which plan best treats integrity as one continuing practice?
body: You want to use what you have learned to handle sources with integrity in your {{context}} work this term. Which plan best treats integrity as one continuing practice?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: You want to use what you have learned to handle sources with integrity in your your subject work this term. Which plan best treats integrity as one continuing practice?

_items.text: With each source, hold the values, reference it with purpose, and judge how to quote or paraphrase, every time.
_items.feedback: Yes. That runs the whole practice, on every source, across the term.

_items.text: Reference everything accurately and leave the values and the judgement aside.
_items.feedback: Accurate referencing alone is the floor; the values and the judgement are part of the practice.

_items.text: Only think about integrity on the one assignment that carries the most marks.
_items.feedback: Integrity is a practice for every source, not only for high-stakes work.

_items.text: Decide once, at the start of term, never to plagiarise, and do nothing more.
_items.feedback: A single decision is not the practice; it runs on each source you use.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Holding the values, referencing with purpose, and judging each source, every time, keeps integrity going as one practice in your {{context}} work.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the plan that runs the values, the purpose and the judgement on every source, over the term.

title: Summative item 7 (tests co4)
displayTitle: Which description best fits academic integrity as one scholarly practice?
body: Which description best fits academic integrity as one scholarly practice?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which description best fits academic integrity as one scholarly practice?

_items.text: Holding the values, referencing with purpose, and judging how to use each source, together, every time.
_items.feedback: Correct.

_items.text: Memorising the rules so you never have to make a judgement.
_items.feedback: The rules follow from the values; the practice still needs judgement.

_items.text: Referencing accurately and thinking no further about the values.
_items.feedback: Accurate referencing is the floor, not the whole practice.

_items.text: Choosing one of the three strands and ignoring the other two.
_items.feedback: The practice holds all three strands together on every source.

_feedback.correct: Correct.

title: Summative item 8 (tests co4)
displayTitle: A student quotes a source where the exact wording matters, credits its author, and can say why the reference strengthens the argument. Which parts of the practice has the student used?
body: A student quotes a source where the exact wording matters, credits its author, and can say why the reference strengthens the argument. Which parts of the practice has the student used?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A student quotes a source where the exact wording matters, credits its author, and can say why the reference strengthens the argument. Which parts of the practice has the student used?

_items.text: The judgement to quote, the values of honest crediting, and the purpose behind the reference, all at once.
_items.feedback: Correct.

_items.text: Only the mark the essay will receive.
_items.feedback: The mark is not the practice; the judgement, the values and the purpose are.

_items.text: Paraphrasing badly to avoid quoting at all.
_items.feedback: The student quoted deliberately, judging that the wording mattered.

_items.text: Referencing only to avoid a plagiarism penalty.
_items.feedback: The student can say why the reference strengthens the argument, which is more than avoiding a penalty.

_feedback.correct: Correct.
